游戏本来的设计方向是成为一款长线运营的在线对战网游，在这一点上它大概算不上成功，到了2026年当下恐怕已经没多少玩家在线打对战了。但实际上，把它当一个单机游戏来玩，游戏本身就非常出色，内容足，易上手难精通，绝对值得喜欢这个类型的玩家购入。

Resolvi testar Faeria porque já jogava Magic: The Gathering e queria algo diferente… e olha, fui surpreendido. O jogo tem uma pegada de cartas, mas mistura com estratégia de tabuleiro de um jeito que no começo você acha que entendeu tudo e, algumas partidas depois, percebe que não entendeu nada mesmo. Ainda assim, é viciante. A arte é linda num nível “abriria o jogo só pra ficar olhando”, e cada partida parece bem única, o que deixa tudo mais interessante. Ao mesmo tempo, não vou fingir que é perfeito: a curva de aprendizado é meio traiçoeira e tem horas que você perde e fica pensando se a culpa foi do jogo… mas geralmente foi sua mesmo. Também senti que a comunidade é menorzinha, então às vezes demora um pouco pra achar partida. No geral, curti bastante a experiência, principalmente por trazer algo diferente do que eu já tava acostumado. Recomendo sim, principalmente se você gosta de jogos de carta e quer testar algo novo, mesmo que isso signifique apanhar um pouco no processo 😅

Played this waaay back on day 1 of its early access release years ago. Came across this again recently on sale and am very glad I picked it up. Still an absolutely fantastic game. Tight gameplay, deep mechanics, and tons of strategy with not only your cards, but land placement, choice, and unit movement. Sequencing your turns becomes incredibly satisfying when all things come together, and is unmatched in other games of the genre like Hearthstone, Gwent, Runeterra, or Elder Scrolls Legends, when that was around.

A very generous and fun solo experience that includes a great draft mode that's fully playable against AI, and a crafting mechanic that lets you craft any cards you want for your deck (with rarer cards becoming craftable as you get into higher levels). Art is warm, bright, and full of whimsy. Music is good and can even be fantastic at times; like when the game knows you're about to win, a chorus will kick off with these nice heavy drums that you can use to time your fatal swing for that oh-so satisfying - THUD - at the end. Some even remind me of Paul Romero tunes.

Overall the game is a pure blast, and quickly sinks its teeth into you (Like coming up with deck ideas when you're trying to sleep). Sure, it's not perfect; you can't re-order the cards in your hand, and some of the art can look out of place (Looking at you Hold the Line!), and the board under your cards can't be interacted with (I'd love to make splishy splashy sounds and bother the Yaks when it's not my turn!), but nothing this game does detracts from its charm or enjoyment. Absolutely recommend to anyone, a really fun CCG from start to finish, and I always feel like playing another round or two.

Faeria, developed by Abrakam Entertainment SA and published by Versus Evil, is a distinctive blend of collectible card game design and turn-based board strategy that sets itself apart from nearly every other title in the genre. Rather than focusing purely on card synergies and resource curves, Faeria introduces a living battlefield where terrain placement, movement, and spatial control are just as important as the cards in your hand. From the outset, the game establishes itself as something more thoughtful and deliberate than a typical digital card battler, rewarding long-term planning and positional awareness over brute-force deck power.

At the heart of Faeria is its hex-based board, which begins each match as an empty expanse of water. Players gradually shape this battlefield by placing land tiles each turn, choosing from different terrain types such as plains, forests, deserts, mountains, and lakes. These terrain choices directly affect which creatures and structures can be played, as many cards require specific land types to exist before they can be summoned. This system transforms every match into a layered strategic puzzle, where players must consider not only what to play, but where and when to expand their territory. Poor terrain decisions early on can limit options later, while clever land placement can enable powerful synergies and restrict an opponent’s movement.

Combat and resource management are deeply intertwined with positioning. Faeria, the game’s primary resource, is generated each turn and supplemented by wells scattered across the board, which provide additional income when creatures stand nearby. This creates constant tension between advancing aggressively to threaten the enemy avatar and holding key positions to maintain resource superiority. Creatures must physically traverse the board to deal damage, making path control, blocking, and terrain denial legitimate tactics. Unlike many card games where damage happens instantly through spells or effects, Faeria often turns combat into a slow, tactical dance where each step forward matters.

Deck building in Faeria emphasizes flexibility and synergy rather than sheer volume of cards. With relatively small deck sizes, every inclusion feels meaningful, and the interaction between terrain requirements and card effects encourages players to think holistically about their strategy. Whether focusing on creature-heavy aggression, spell-based control, or mobility and positioning tricks, successful decks are those that can adapt to changing board states. The game’s design ensures that matches are rarely decided by luck alone; thoughtful sequencing and spatial foresight tend to outweigh fortunate draws.

For solo-focused players, Faeria offers a surprisingly robust suite of content. Tutorials, challenges, and puzzle modes gradually introduce mechanics while encouraging creative problem-solving. These puzzles are particularly effective at teaching advanced concepts, often presenting scenarios that require precise positioning and clever use of limited resources. The Pandora mode, a roguelike-style draft experience, adds another layer of replayability by forcing players to adapt to unpredictable card pools and terrain constraints, testing strategic fundamentals rather than reliance on perfected decks.

Multiplayer is where Faeria’s systems truly shine, as human opponents bring unpredictability and psychological depth to terrain placement and movement. Ranked and casual matches reward players who can read their opponent’s intentions and anticipate future expansions of the board. Because the battlefield is shared and mutable, every decision influences both players, creating a sense of constant interaction even during defensive turns. Matches often feel like extended duels of positioning rather than explosive bursts of action, which gives victories a satisfying sense of earned mastery.

Visually, Faeria adopts a clean, vibrant fantasy style that complements its strategic focus. The animated board feels alive as terrain spreads outward, and card art is colorful and expressive without overwhelming the interface. Sound design is understated but effective, reinforcing the calm, thoughtful pace of play rather than pushing constant excitement. The presentation supports the game’s identity as a cerebral strategy experience rather than a fast-paced spectacle.

Faeria is not without its challenges. The learning curve can be demanding, especially for players accustomed to more streamlined card games where positioning plays a minimal role. Understanding how terrain decisions ripple through future turns takes time, and early mistakes can feel punishing until players fully grasp the system. Additionally, its emphasis on strategic depth over spectacle means it may not appeal to those seeking quick, flashy matches or heavy narrative elements.

Overall, Faeria stands as one of the most inventive digital card games available on Steam, offering a rare fusion of board control and deck construction that feels genuinely fresh. Its emphasis on spatial strategy, deliberate pacing, and meaningful decision-making gives it remarkable longevity for players willing to invest the time to master its mechanics. For fans of thoughtful strategy games who enjoy planning several turns ahead and shaping the battlefield as much as their deck, Faeria delivers a rich and deeply rewarding experience that continues to stand out in a crowded genre.

昔、コンシューマーゲームであったポケモンカードGBや遊戯王のような気軽にCPU戦を楽しみながらカード集めていくようなゲームを探していました。
このゲームはかなり自分の求めていたものに近かったです！

ソロだけではなく、もちろんランクマッチも可能で人口も少ないながらも居ます。

もともとは課金要素もあったみたいなんですが、現在では買い切りの形になっています。
ゲームを遊んでいくとプレイヤーレベルが上がり、その報酬でバトルチェスト（ブースターパック）が引けます。
カードはデッキに入れられる上限を超えると出現しなくなるため、いつかは集めきることができる作りになってます。

また、6時間毎にコモン・レア・エピックのカードを生成することができるので、欲しいカードは比較的集めやすいです。
・コモンはユーザーレベル５から生成可能
・レアはユーザーレベル１０から生成可能
・エピックはユーザーレベル１５から生成可能

Gostei bastante da dinâmica de montar um deck de cartas e de expandir os territórios. A arte das cartas também são bem bonitas e há diferentes estratégicas que pode fazer. No momento só joguei off line: missões, aventuras e quebra-cabeças. Curti o jogo!

Por mais estranho que pareça, há algo mágico em jogar Faeria mesmo nos dias de hoje. Um jogo que, apesar de estar abandonado há anos, ainda consegue ser surpreendentemente aconchegante, cheio de vida e estratégias únicas que o destacam no mar de card games por aí.

Conheci Faeria tardiamente — muito tempo após seu auge e bem depois de seu último suspiro de suporte oficial, que aconteceu em 2021. E mesmo assim, ele me conquistou. 

Ao contrário de muitos TCGs tradicionais, Faeria mistura elementos de tabuleiro e estratégia territorial, o que transforma cada partida em uma verdadeira partida de xadrez místico com criaturas e terrenos mágicos. Você não joga apenas cartas... você constrói o campo de batalha sob seus pés, literalmente moldando o cenário para ganhar vantagem.

Essa mecânica de "terraformar" o tabuleiro faz com que o jogo seja mais tático e interativo do que a maioria dos card games digitais modernos, que geralmente se limitam a apenas posicionar cartas e torcer para o RNG te favorecer. Aqui, o posicionamento e o planejamento de terrenos viram parte essencial do gameplay. E isso, por si só, já faz Faeria ser uma preciosidade no gênero. 

Outro ponto que me surpreendeu foi o conteúdo solo. Faeria oferece campanhas, desafios, quebra-cabeças e modos PvE que realmente valem o tempo. Diferente de muitos card games que colocam o solo como um mero tutorial, aqui você sente que há conteúdo pensado com carinho.

Os puzzles, por exemplo, são engenhosos. Te forçam a pensar de forma criativa e aprendem as mecânicas de maneira prática. É viciante resolver um após o outro. 

É triste saber que esse jogo incrível foi deixado de lado. Desde 2021 não há nenhuma atualização, e a desenvolvedora (Abrakam) simplesmente seguiu para outros projetos. Ver algo tão promissor ser abandonado assim machuca um pouquinho, ainda mais quando se pensa em tudo que poderia ter sido.

Mas, por outro lado, fico com o coração quentinho ao ver que Faeria ainda possui uma comunidade fiel, ativa, e que se recusa a deixá-lo morrer. Mesmo sem updates, sempre há alguém online para uma partida. Isso me faz sorrir. 🥲❤️

Faeria, com seus visuais suaves, trilha sonora calma e jogabilidade fluida, se tornou meu jogo conforto. Sempre que quero relaxar, pensar em estratégias e esquecer o mundo lá fora, ele tá lá, firme e forte me recebendo com um "bem-vinda de volta".

Mesmo sendo um "jogo abandonado", Faeria tem alma. E é justamente essa alma que me faz voltar, mesmo que a cada partida eu me pergunte o que teria sido se ele tivesse recebido o amor e reconhecimento que merece.

As strange as it may sound, there's something magical about playing Faeria even today. A game that, despite being abandoned for years, still manages to feel incredibly cozy, full of life, and packed with unique strategies that make it stand out in the vast sea of card games.

I discovered Faeria quite late — long after its prime and well past its last official update, which happened back in 2021. And yet, it completely won me over. 

Unlike most traditional TCGs, Faeria mixes board game elements and territorial strategy, turning every match into a mystical chess-like battle with magical creatures and living terrain. You’re not just playing cards… you’re literally building the battlefield beneath your feet, shaping the map to your advantage.

This "terraforming" mechanic makes the game far more tactical and interactive than most modern digital card games, which often come down to playing cards and praying to the RNG gods. In Faeria, positioning and land planning are key parts of the gameplay. And that alone makes it a hidden gem within the genre. 

Another thing that truly impressed me was the solo content. Faeria offers campaigns, challenges, puzzles, and PvE modes that are actually worth your time. Unlike many card games that treat solo content as just a glorified tutorial, here you can feel that the single-player experience was designed with real care and love.

The puzzles, for example, are brilliant. They force you to think creatively and teach the mechanics in clever, engaging ways. It's addictive to solve one after another. 

It’s heartbreaking to know that such a wonderful game was left behind. No updates have been released since 2021, and the developers (Abrakam) have moved on to other projects. Seeing something with so much potential abandoned like this hurts a little — especially when you imagine all that it could have become.

But on the flip side, my heart warms up every time I see that Faeria still has a loyal, active community that refuses to let it die. Even without updates, you’ll still find someone online ready for a match. And that makes me smile. 

With its soft visuals, calming soundtrack, and smooth gameplay, Faeria has become my comfort game. Whenever I want to relax, think strategically, and forget the world outside for a while, it’s there for me — steady and strong, welcoming me back with open arms.

Even though it’s considered an “abandoned game,” Faeria has soul. And it's exactly that soul that keeps pulling me back — even if, with every match, I can’t help but wonder what might have been if it had received the love and recognition it truly deserves.

Pessoalmente, eu prefiro escrever resenhas sobre jogos que joguei por mais tempo. No entanto, acredito que jogarei Faeria por muito tempo. Vou explicar o que ele tem de bom.

Inicialmente, eu estava em busca de um jogo de cartas ou estratégia que pudesse jogar sozinho. Infelizmente, jogos como Magic se tornaram apenas formas das empresas arrancarem dinheiro com o nervosismo e a impaciência dos jogadores "fre to play". No Magic, por exemplo, você pode montar um deck com suas cartas coringas que ganha no tutorial de novo jogador. Mas se precisar de dois ou três decks devido a uma rotação de cartas ou banimento, você enfrentará dificuldades. Será necessário muitas horas para obter as cartas necessárias. Enquanto isso, você vira saco de pancada de quem investe dinheiro no jogo.

Buscando evitar essa experiência, encontrei alternativas, e entre elas, Faeria se destacou. Comprei o jogo não para jogar com outros, mas para jogar sozinho. Pesquisei em fóruns e percebi que a experiência solo é muito satisfatória. No início, pode parecer que o jogo está vazio, mas não está. Ainda há pessoas jogando, especialmente nos consoles. Mas meu foco é jogar sozinho.

Comprei todas as expansões disponíveis para progredir mais rápido e ter mais conteúdo para o modo solo. Até agora, joguei apenas três horas, mas já percebi que o jogo tem muito a oferecer. Os gráficos são bonitos e a música é agradável, permitindo que você jogue sem precisar de outra trilha sonora. Os controles são fáceis, e uso um controle de Xbox, pois prefiro jogar longe da tela do computador. O jogo é totalmente adaptado para o controle.

Nos modos de jogo, há missões diárias contra a inteligência artificial, que é desafiadora, mas vencível com paciência. Há também missões de pacotes que você pode completar, além de outros modos que ainda não explorei. Isso mostra que há muita progressão para o jogador solo.

A jogabilidade de Faeria é simples. É um jogo de cartas por turnos, mas você também monta um campo de batalha. A cada turno, você pode colocar dois espaços no campo, ou um espaço especial, similar à mana especializada do Magic. É crucial planejar a colocação dos terrenos para evitar que o inimigo convoque monstros perto da sua base. O jogo requer estratégia e planejamento. As cartas são bonitas e lembram as do Hearthstone, mas com arte mais caprichada e efeitos interessantes. Há sinergias e arquétipos para montar seus decks.

Faeria é um jogo completo. Além da campanha, oferece modos como quebra-cabeça e um sistema de drafting, similar ao do Magic. Richard Garfield, um dos consultores na criação do jogo, contribuiu para sua maturidade. Felizmente, o jogo não teve sucesso em eSports, o que levou ao desenvolvimento de mais conteúdo para o jogador solo. Isso é ótimo, pois jogos free-to-play com foco competitivo geralmente não duram.

O jogo ainda está ativo, com excelente conteúdo para um jogador. Recomendo muito a compra de Faeria, especialmente em promoção. Vale muito a pena.

Faeria is fun. Okay, I can see myself spending 10 more hours on fighting AI on Pandora Mode. I already spent 28 hours. The rest of the game depends if I can push myself over the skill cliff of deckbuilding, because it's really hard. I can recommend this game very easily. I get to max out the utility of every monster, every decision, and win a lot.

But let's go into the reasons why this game isn't successful. NOTE: I go against AI and don't really compete.
- Faeria looks like a typo to a lot of search engines. It's very close to Fairy.
- You don't get to walk around. Like every other trading card game, you battle and these battles can get lengthy. There's no rest stop besides staring at the card collection.
- The campaign mode is fighting random NPCs with one-liners and that's it. There's no story, no satisfying closures besides winning, no secrets to unlock beyond the loot boxes of cards. The boss battles do have that unfair advantage, but there's no extra flair to them so they still look like normal NPCs to fight. While you are building a card collection, most people won't feel the dopamine of progress.
- In a fair match, the tension is not there for a lot of mid games. You either steamroll or get steamrolled. This might be because I play very defensively and haven't touched the aggressive cards. This might also be b/c I don't play competitively. I like steamrolling, but variety is the spice of life.
- Most of us will never ever beat this game, because the hard challenges are really hard. Many games can split the difficulty into Easy Mode, Normal Mode, and Hard Mode. This game doesn't split those modes, it blends them all together (easy stuff first ofc) and you know, not everyone wants to play Hard Mode. Like I said, my next 10 hours are probably going to be Pandora Mode and ignore the rest of it.
- I've fallen into playing very defensively. Like I ALWAYS go for the faeria well on the first turn. This might be a me problem, but I feel like it's the strongest strat.

What is Pandora Mode? You build a random deck 1 card at a time and play 6 random NPCs in a FAIR match. And there's rewards for it.

But again, I like the game. But again, I like utilizing every card to the most of its ability, being very goal-orientated when I place new land, and then steamrolling my AI opponents.

The ability to select and place lands on the board provides so many strategic considerations.  It's also interesting that having presence on the board is rewarded, with additional options for land placement and "faeria" (this game's version of "mana" or "energy") if positioned correctly.  If the overall flow of card games and/or the art presented above inspire appeal, this is probably worth playing.  I habitually refuse to engage in micro-transactions or purchase DLC content, but I've been enjoying this enough that I made an exception (when they went on sale, of course).

I have not thoroughly investigated PvP, so I can't speak to any meta or the overall balance of power among cards, but I successfully got in a few matches with ease.  There is a wealth of solo content to be completed, some of which unlocks additional cards.  Additionally, one is able to craft some new cards each day (one card per six hours, after a certain early player level, at time of writing).  Packs are obtained from leveling up and completing daily given quests, which can be rerolled once if you would like a different task than the one it presents.  There's a draft mode ("Pandora" it's called) which I have yet to touch after almost 80 hours logged.

I would recommend this wholeheartedly, with a few caveats.  First, know that there is unlikely to be any new content; there hasn't been a balance patch in years.  The developers are openly working on other, newer projects.  Secondly, to get the most of your play time and unlock cards efficiently, it might be best to play regularly/daily rather than dedicating isolated, longer blocks of time.
